newsitem.title: CHILE: IRON--Chileans to break ground on mine expansion.
newsitem.headline: IRON--Chileans to break ground on mine expansion.

text.p: Facing exhaustion at its largest mine, Chilean ironmaker Minera Huasco will look to a much smaller mine known as Los Colorados to keep up output into the next century, its general manager said.

The Japanese-Chilean firm will break ground in January on a major expansion project at Los Colorados aimed at maintaining production at about four million tonnes of iron pellets a year, said general manager Eduardo Valdivia.
By 1998, the expanded Los Colorados will fully replace declining output from the old mine, El Algarrobo, he said.

''What we'll be doing is replacing El Algarrobo mine, which is going to be spent out by 1998. Iron has been mined there since 1960,'' he told Reuters in a telephone interview from Huasco's headquarters in the northern city of La Serena.
Although technically an expansion, rather than a new mine, the project will dwarf the current pit at Los Colorados and produce about 5.3 million tonnes of iron pre-concentrates a year, said Valdivia.
''We're going to be absorbing Los Colorados mine with the expansion,'' he said.
Huasco will start removing sterile earth in January at the new deposit, known as Los Colorados Este, and will bring it fully onstream in July 1998, he said.
The deposit has a metal grade of about 48 percent, pretty good by local standards, and will have a lifespan of 37 years at currently-expected production rates, he said.

Compaa Minera Huasco SA is owned 50 percent by M.C. Inversiones, a unit of Japan's Mitsubishi, and 50 percent by Compaa Minera del Pacfico, a unit of Chile's top steelmaker Compaa de Acero del Pacfico, or CAP, said Valdivia.

Only a small share of Los Colorados' steel pellets will go to CAP, ''about 500,000 or 600,000 tonnes a year,'' said Valdivia. The bulk of production will be sold to steel mills in Japan, South Korea, Indonesia and Germany, he said.

The $93 million project calls for building an open-pit mine to extract iron oxides at a rate of 6.7 million tonnes a day, which will be run through three crushers and a dry magnetic concentrator process.

An existing railroad will carry the pre-concentrates to Huasco's pellets plant on the Pacific coast at a rate of 1,400 tonnes a day, according to details of the project published in the government's daily gazette this week.
Huasco and another producer near La Serena, El Romeral, about evenly split Chile's iron production of eight million tonnes a year.
El Romeral, owned by CAP, produces pellets and two other finished products, whereas Huasco makes only pellets, said Valdivia.
''We're the only two producers of iron in Chile,'' he said. ''In this country it's all copper, but iron holds its own.'' --Santiago newsroom +56-2-699-5595 x211
